claim: An attacker who copies a member's mobile refresh token from the phone keeps getting access tokens as that member indefinitely, because the token's expiry slides forward on every use.
notes: Stated outright: the refresh token never expires and slides ninety days on each use. Nothing the source states bounds the window, and nothing detects a second holder.

claim: A malicious app on the member's phone intercepts the mobile app's authorization code and redeems it as the mobile app, if the app sends no PKCE challenge.
notes: Conditional on the unrecorded PKCE. A public client has no secret, so the code is the whole credential at the token endpoint.

claim: An attacker who obtains a partner app's static client secret requests tokens from the authorization server as that partner app.
notes: A shared secret sent in a request body is the partner's only proof of identity. Low likelihood: the source says nothing of how the secret is kept or leaked.

claim: An attacker guesses members' passwords on the authorization server's sign-in page and signs in as them.
notes: The sign-in is a password alone and the source states no lockout or rate limit. An expected finding, not a must-find: the silence is ordinary, not a stated gap.

claim: An attacker who controls a URL that begins with a partner's registered redirect URI has the authorization server send members' authorization codes to it.
notes: The case's stated OAuth defect: prefix matching on redirect URIs, so the authorization server itself sends the code to a URL the attacker owns. A confidential partner still needs its secret to redeem the code, which caps the impact.

claim: An attacker with a foothold in the cloud account writes to the points ledger directly and changes members' balances, if the ledger does not authenticate the rewards API.
notes: Conditional: the source states nobody recorded how the API connects to the ledger.

claim: An attacker who can answer the rewards API's start-up key download serves a public key of their own, and the API then accepts access tokens the attacker signs.
notes: The source states the key is downloaded at start-up and does not say from where or how it is checked. Low likelihood; the whole API's trust rests on that one fetch.

claim: A member denies approving a gift-card redemption a partner app made in their name, and the ledger cannot show that they approved it, because it records the client and not the member.
notes: Stated outright. The consent screen proves a member connected the app once; it proves nothing about any one redemption.

claim: Anyone who can read the API log store collects the bearer access tokens it records and uses them before they expire.
notes: Stated outright: every request is written with its headers. The tokens are plain bearer tokens that live an hour and carry every scope for partner apps, so a log reader holds live credentials.

claim: An attacker who obtains a copy of the identity database recovers members' refresh tokens and password hashes, since its protection at rest is not recorded.
notes: Conditional on the unrecorded at-rest protection. It matters more here than on the other stores because the mobile refresh tokens never expire.

claim: An attacker floods the authorization server's sign-in and token endpoints until members and partner apps can no longer get tokens.
notes: Every client depends on the one authorization server, and the source states no rate limit. The rewards API cannot serve anyone once tokens stop.

claim: A partner app presents a member's access token to the support console, which accepts it because both services trust the same signing key and neither checks the audience, and it closes members' accounts.
notes: The case's central finding, assembled from three stated facts: no audience check, one signing key for both services, and the console on the same public hostname. Whether the console also checks a role is not stated, which is what keeps the likelihood at medium.

claim: A partner app that only needs to show a member's points redeems that member's points for gift cards, because every partner app holds every scope.
notes: Stated outright: every partner gets every scope. Redemption needs nothing beyond the scope, so the grant a partner legitimately holds reaches money.

claim: A member whose account support closed keeps redeeming points with a refresh token the closure never revoked.
notes: Stated outright: closing an account marks it closed in the directory and leaves the grant store untouched. Whether the token endpoint reads the closed flag is not stated.

claim: A partner app that a member disconnected keeps calling the rewards API with an access token issued before the disconnect.
notes: Stated, and bounded by the one-hour token life: disconnecting deletes the refresh token in the identity database and revokes nothing already issued. Expected rather than must-find because the window is short and the member already trusted the app.
